content: An emulsion is a mixture of two substances that do not naturally blend together, known as immiscible substances. In an emulsion, one substance, referred to as the dispersed phase, is distributed within another substance, called the continuous phase. Examples of emulsions include butter, margarine, milk, cream, espresso, mayonnaise, photographic film coatings, magmas, and cutting fluids used in metalworking. In butter and margarine, water droplets are surrounded by oil, forming a water-in-oil emulsion. Conversely, in milk and cream, oil droplets are surrounded by water, creating an oil-in-water emulsion. In certain types of magma, liquid nickel-iron globules may be dispersed within a continuous phase of liquid silicates. The process of creating an emulsion is called emulsification. In the oil industry, the term emulsion can also refer to untreated well production that primarily consists of crude oil and water. Emulsions typically appear cloudy due to the scattering of light at the interfaces between the dispersed and continuous phases. These systems are inherently unstable and do not form spontaneously. Energy input, such as shaking, stirring, homogenization, or spraying, is required to create an emulsion. Over time, emulsions tend to separate into their stable states, with oil and water separating. However, the addition of surface-active agents, or surfactants, can significantly enhance the kinetic stability of emulsions, allowing them to remain unchanged for years. For example, homemade oil-and-vinegar salad dressing is an unstable emulsion that separates quickly unless continuously shaken. This separation process, known as coalescence, occurs when smaller droplets merge to form larger ones. Emulsions can also experience creaming, where one substance migrates to the top of the emulsion due to buoyancy or centrifugal forces. Emulsions belong to a broader category of two-phase systems called colloids. While the terms colloid and emulsion are sometimes used interchangeably, emulsions specifically involve both the dispersed and continuous phases being liquids. Emulsion instability can manifest in three ways: flocculation, where particles clump together; creaming, where particles concentrate at the surface or bottom of the mixture while remaining separate; and breaking or coalescence, where particles merge to form a distinct liquid layer. An emulsifier, also known as an emulgent, is a substance that stabilizes an emulsion, often by acting as a surfactant. Common food emulsifiers include egg yolk, which contains lecithin, as well as honey and mustard, which contain various emulsifying chemicals. Proteins and low-molecular-weight emulsifiers are also frequently used. In some cases, particles can stabilize emulsions through a mechanism called Pickering stabilization. Examples of emulsions stabilized by egg yolk lecithin include mayonnaise and hollandaise sauce, both of which are oil-in-water emulsions. Detergents, another class of surfactants, chemically interact with both oil and water, stabilizing the interface between oil and water droplets. This principle is utilized in soap to remove grease during cleaning. In pharmacy, a wide range of emulsifiers are employed to prepare emulsions such as creams and lotions. Whether an emulsion becomes a water-in-oil or oil-in-water emulsion depends on the volume fraction of the phases and the type of emulsifier used. According to the Bancroft rule, emulsifiers tend to promote the dispersion of the phase in which they are less soluble. For instance, proteins, which dissolve better in water than in oil, tend to form oil-in-water emulsions by dispersing oil droplets throughout a continuous water phase. A nanoemulsion is a specialized type of emulsion in which the dispersed phase consists of particles smaller than 1000 nanometers. In medicine, a nanoemulsion of soybean oil can create droplets measuring 400–600 nanometers in diameter, which are capable of killing many pathogens, including bacteria and viruses. This process is physical rather than chemical, relying on the high surface tension of the small droplets to exert force on lipid membranes. The oil is emulsified with detergents to stabilize the droplets, preventing them from merging. When these droplets encounter the lipid membranes of bacteria or viruses, they force the lipids to merge with themselves, effectively disintegrating the membrane and killing the pathogen. Remarkably, this type of soybean oil nanoemulsion does not harm normal human cells or the cells of most higher organisms, with the exception of sperm cells and blood cells, which are vulnerable due to their membrane structures. For this reason, such nanoemulsions are not yet suitable for intravenous use. The most effective application of this type of nanoemulsion is for disinfecting surfaces. Certain nanoemulsions have been shown to effectively destroy pathogens such as HIV-1 and tuberculosis bacteria on non-porous surfaces.
